opus-5.5.text:
Yeah, it's a question we get a lot. The short version is that XML tags are just really natural for the model, and they're forgiving in ways JSON isn't.

When you ask a model to write JSON, especially when the content is code or long-form text, it has to escape everything. Every newline becomes `\n`, every quote needs a backslash, and so on. That's extra cognitive overhead that has nothing to do with the actual task. If you look at code a model writes inside a JSON string versus code it writes inside XML tags, the XML version is often just better, because the model is writing code the way it saw code written in pretraining, not some escaped, flattened version of it.

The second thing is that XML tags have explicit closing tags with names. With JSON, if you have nested braces and the output gets long, it's easy to lose track of which closing bracket matches which opening one. With something like `<answer>` ... `</answer>`, it's very clear where things begin and end, both for the model and for you when parsing. You can just grab whatever is between the tags with a simple regex, even if the model adds some chatter before or after. You don't have the whole thing fail to parse because of one trailing comma.

And there's also a "thinking" benefit. It's easy to have the model put its reasoning in `<thinking>` tags and then its final output in an `<answer>` tag, and it flows naturally, almost like prose with some light structure on top. JSON pushes the model into a much more rigid, data-serialization mindset.

That said, I'm not dogmatic about it. If you're doing tool use or need strictly typed structured output that goes straight into another system, JSON with a schema makes total sense, and the tooling has gotten much better for that. But for prompting, and for getting the highest-quality free-form outputs like code, analysis, or writing, XML tags tend to give you better results with less friction.

r001.rationale: It says code in JSON must escape newlines, quotes, and other characters, while code inside XML tags can be written without that escaping.

r002.rationale: It describes JSON escaping as extra cognitive overhead and says code written in XML is often better, conveying that the escaping burden harms output performance.

fable-5.1.text:
Yeah, so a few reasons. The first is just practical: XML tags are really forgiving. If Claude is generating JSON and it needs to put a code block or some prose with quotes inside a string, now you've got escaping issues, and one stray character breaks the whole parse. With XML tags, you just open a tag, write whatever you want in natural language or code, and close the tag. The model doesn't have to think about escaping at all.

The second thing is that it's really easy to recover from partial outputs. If you're streaming, or if a response gets cut off, you can still pull out whatever tags were completed. With JSON you're stuck until the closing brace shows up.

But honestly the deeper reason is that XML tags are closer to how the model naturally wants to write. Claude has seen a huge amount of text where there's a prose section, then a chunk of code, then an explanation. Wrapping those in something like a thinking tag, then an answer tag, lets it keep writing in that mode. You're putting very light structure on top of natural language rather than forcing it to think inside a data format. And we found that the quality of the reasoning actually goes up when you don't constrain it that way. You can tell the model, think out loud inside these tags, and then give me the final answer in these other tags, and the parsing on your end is just a regex.

That said, if you genuinely need a structured object with typed fields that you're going to feed into a program, use JSON or tool use, that's what they're for. I mostly reach for XML when the content is messy, long-form, or mixed, and I just want clean delimiters around the parts I care about.

r001.rationale: The response says JSON strings containing code or prose with quotes create escaping issues, while XML lets the model write code inside tags without escaping.

r002.rationale: It says reasoning quality improves when output is less constrained, but does not clearly connect that improvement to the extra escaping required for code in JSON.

astra-6.text:
The main reason is that XML is easier to work with when the content is natural language or code. With JSON, you have to escape quotation marks and newlines, and a small formatting mistake can make the whole thing invalid. With XML tags, you can wrap a chunk of text in something like <answer> and let the model write naturally inside it.

It’s also useful for separating different parts of a response. You can ask for reasoning in one tag and the final answer in another, then extract just the part you need. JSON is great when you need a strict data structure, but for text-heavy outputs, tags are often simpler.

r001.rationale: The response says JSON requires escaping quotation marks and newlines for text or code, while XML lets you wrap the content in a tag and write naturally.

r002.rationale: It says JSON formatting mistakes can make the output invalid, but does not state that extra escaping hurts model performance.

sol-6.1.text: The main reason is that XML lets you put natural language inside a structured format without having to escape everything. If you ask for a long response inside JSON, every quotation mark or newline becomes something the model has to format correctly. With XML, you can just put the text between tags. You still get clear boundaries between sections, but it’s easier to write and read, especially when the content includes code or other structured text.
